transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
11 people were killed in a firefight last night as Mexican authorities captured one of the most wanted drug lords in the country.
NPR's Zeta Peralto reports he was on the FBI's "10 Most Wanted" list.
Pausto Isidro Mesaflores, who was better known as El Chapo Isidro, is the leader of the Beltranleva cartel.
The U.S. accuses him of running huge quantities of drugs, including meth and fentanyl, to the U.S.
The Mexican military says it captured Mesaflores in Wasave, Sinaloa, using U.S. intelligence.
Residents reported that the military fired from helicopters while the cartels burned cars and trucks.
A baseball game was disrupted by the heavy fighting and some residents had to spend the night at a supermarket to stay safe.
Over the past couple of years, as the U.S. has mounted pressure on Mexico to fight organized crime,
security forces have captured a number of drug lords.
The power vacuums have often led to an increase in violence.
Ayur Peralto, NPR News, Mexico City.
President Trump made history this week with the first trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia
on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Summit in Shenzhen, China.
But whether there will be an immediate or lasting impact isn't certain.
And here's Ron Elving has more on if the meeting has any real-world consequences.
It could have if these various vows of peaceful cooperation bear fruit or if these vaunted trade deals come to pass.
But what we do know at this point is that Russia this week launched one of its most massive assaults against Ukraine
since it first invaded that country in 2022,
assaults against civilian targets that also struck Poland, a NATO alloy of the U.S.
And it makes a difference that Trump was more interested in meeting with Chinese President Xi
than he was in confronting that country's efforts to obtain the most advanced American computer chips.
And here's Ron Elving reporting.
A judge has ruled that the Trump administration's plan to overhaul funding for homeless programs is unlawful.
In Paris, Jennifer Ludden reports, HUD wants to shift money away from programs that support permanent housing.
The decision is the latest setback for the Trump administration's push to fund more transitional housing with mandated treatment for addiction.
The ruling found that doing so would exceed HUD's authority and go against requirements set by Congress.
The judge also struck down a restriction on so-called harm reduction efforts like offering clean needle exchanges for drug users.
Democratic-led states and homeless advocacy groups brought the suit and argued that long-term housing without preconditions has a long track record of success.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner disputes that claim and told Reuters the agency reserves the right to appeal.
The court ruling comes just over a week before the deadline when local providers must apply for federal grants.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR News.
A mathematician and anthropic says he may have solved what's been called the holy grail of math problems with help from the company's chatbot, Claude.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports the remand hypothesis has been an open question for more than 160 years.
Rutgers University mathematician Alex Controvich says he never expected to see a proof of the remand hypothesis in his lifetime.
I thought I was done picking myself up off the floor, and I'm shocked, and I'm still shocked.
The hypothesis describes how prime numbers are spread out, and getting to a solution means drawing on decades of work across different branches of mathematics.
The new claim involves just massive, massive amounts of mathematics. There's no human being that has all of that in their head.
Teams of human mathematicians will now examine parts of the computer code and piece together how the proof works.
Controvich says understanding the proposed proof from anthropic could take months.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh swam the Strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental threats during ongoing conflicts.
Pugh, who's a U.N. patron of the oceans, completed the swim this week despite nearby attacks on vessels,
saying he felt explosions and saw a tanker get hit.
And he says oil pollution from damaged tankers threatens the area's wildlife and ecosystems.
Over his 40-year career, Pugh has used his swims to advocate for the protection of seas and rivers.
This is NPR.

Trump holds first trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Putin at APEC summit in Shenzhen
Russia launches a major assault on Ukraine that also struck targets in Poland
Judge rules Trump administration's HUD homeless funding overhaul unlawful, blocks harm reduction restrictions
Anthropic mathematician claims proof of the Riemann hypothesis with help from Claude chatbot
Endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh swims Strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental threats from conflict
